bounds: Dilution happens when a company issues new shares or securities that convert into shares, so an existing holder owns a smaller percentage of the total.
It does not automatically mean the company is worth less.
Imagine you own 100 shares out of 1,000, or 10%.
If the company later issues 500 new shares and you receive none, you still hold 100 shares, but now there are 1,500 total.
Those new shares might help fund growth, but the outcome depends on how the money is used and what the company becomes worth.
SAFEs, convertible notes, employee options, and new financing rounds can all affect the share count.
Some preferred shares may carry rights that differ from common shares.
When reviewing an offering, look at the current capitalization table and ask what securities could convert or be issued later.
A percentage today is not necessarily your percentage after future financing.
